newsitem.title: UK: Jury to decide if UK warcrimes trial proceeds.
newsitem.headline: Jury to decide if UK warcrimes trial proceeds.

text.p: A jury will decide if an 85-year-old refugee accused of killing Jews during World War Two should face Britain's first war crimes trial, a judge ruled on Friday.
Judge Humphrey Potts set two preliminary hearings for the case against Szymon Serafinowicz.
The first, beginning on December 17, will decide whether the case is an "abuse of process" because it takes place more than 50 years after the alleged crimes took place.
The second will decide whether the frail former carpenter is fit to stand trial. This stage is due to begin on January 7 and last for seven days.
If the jury agrees that the full trial can take place it will begin on January 22 at London's central criminal court.
Serafinowicz's defence team will argue that he is unfit to face a six-week trial and that the case should be dismissed.
A tiny, grey-haired man in a shabby fawn-coloured jacket, the former carpenter sat in the dock during Friday's hearing, rocking gently in his seat and occasionally seeming to grimace.
He is partially deaf and could not hear when a court clerk asked him to sit down.
An unconfirmed newspaper report said last week that he is suffering from Alzheimer's disease, which causes dementia.
Serafinowciz is accused of killing three Jews between 1941 and 1942 while Byelorussia, now Belarus, was under German occupation.
His defence requested at least two weeks gap between the second preliminary hearing and the full trial because many of the elderly witnesses would have to travel to London.

"Witnesses will have to be brought in the middle of a Byelorussian winter over very difficult terrain," said William Clegg. Other witnesses are expected to be brought from countries around the world, including Israel and South Africa.
The defence also argues that it would be unfair to rely on the evidence of elderly witnesses about events that happened more than 50 years ago.

Like many Byelorussians hostile to Soviet rule, Serafinowicz joined a police force set up by the Nazi occupiers during World War Two and he became the commander of a unit accused of torturing and killing Jews.
His trial is being held under Britain's controversial war crimes act, which the government had to invoke special powers to force through parliament in 1991.
It allows the prosecution of accused war criminals even though they are not British citizens and their offences took place outside British territory.
